title: The elephant facing north
hook: the search; the head; the boy lives

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva came home, and a boy lost his head at the door. Your line was what broke can be mended. Today, the mending. Day twenty-four.

Shiva gives an order to his ganas: go north. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. So they run, down off the mountain, into the forests, heading north. And the first creature they find is an elephant. In the version most families tell, it's lying asleep with its head toward the north. They bring the head back. Shiva sets it on the boy's body, and breathes life into him, and the boy opens his eyes, for the second time in his life. His mother is there again. But now he has a trunk, and wide ears, and a face every child in India can draw by the age of four.
screen: `GO NORTH.` → `THE FIRST CREATURE YOU MEET.` → `AN ELEPHANT.` → `HE OPENS HIS EYES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: People ask, fairly: why an elephant? The story's plain answer is: it was the first creature they met. But Hindus have been finding meaning in that face for a long time. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A small mouth. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up a single grain of rice. An elephant doesn't go around the forest. It walks through, and makes a path. That's why Ganesha is called the remover of obstacles. You met that on day one. Now you know where the face came from. The versions differ, and it's worth saying so. The Shiva Purana tells it as you heard it: north, the first creature. Popular tellings add the sleeping elephant with its head to the north. Another text, the Brahmavaivarta Purana, tells a different story, where the head is lost for another reason entirely. The tradition keeps them side by side. Here's the part that matters most. When the boy wakes, Shiva doesn't just forgive him. He honors him. He makes him the leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him. That's his name: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas. And Shiva makes a promise, with all the gods listening: this boy will be worshipped first. Before any other god. Before any ceremony. So to this day, a Hindu wedding, a housewarming, a new business, a first day of school, often starts with Ganesha. First, before anyone. The boy who was killed at the door becomes the one who opens every door.
screen: `WHY AN ELEPHANT?` · `BIG EARS, A PATH THROUGH.` · `THE VERSIONS DIFFER.` · `WORSHIPPED FIRST, BEFORE ANY GOD.` · then, large: `FIRST, BEFORE ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gratitude for a mend in your life. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that broke, and came back different, but whole. A friendship after a fight. A body after an injury. You, after a hard year. Maybe it came back with a new face, like the boy. Just thank it, or thank whoever helped mend it. If you pray, you can say thank you to God. The bell holds the time.
The elephant facing north. The first creature found, whose head brought the boy back to life, and a promise: he'll be honored first.
Your line: first, before anyone. Today, begin one thing well: before the first email, the first bite, the first word, pause for one breath. Day twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

original.note: Sanskrit: elephant (gaja) face (anana), one of Ganesha's names.

trapdoor: what you thought: a god with an elephant head, because why not.
what it means: a boy brought back to life with a new face, and honored first before every god.
what a scholar hears: Ganapati, lord of the ganas, is an old title; the versions of how he got his head differ between the Puranas, and the tradition keeps both.
